_what: The hand-kept half of the launch readiness report. readiness.py reads this and writes READINESS.md; nothing generated ever writes this file. Two lists: errors a person knows about, and how far each part of the site has been taken. Both exist because they cannot be measured off disk -- an error nobody has noticed is not in here, and no script can tell a first draft from a second.
_how_to_use: Add an error the moment it is found, with status open. When it is fixed, set status to fixed, put the commit in fixed_by, and name the preflight check that now guards it -- or say none, which is itself worth seeing. Move a feature to draft 2 only after it has actually been gone over, not after it has been touched.
_status_values: error.status: open | fixed | source_gap. feature.draft: 1 | 2 | unreviewed.

24 current-term bills where bill_text.json's version disagrees with the database's newest printing, two of them showing a fiscal note where the database holds the introduced bill. MEASURED 22 September, and 22 of the 24 were not an error at all. The comparison behind the number ranked a bill's printings by DocumentVersion.SortOrder, which is a stage order and not a chronological one -- 'As Amended by the House (2nd committee)' is 50 and 'As Amended by the Senate' is 30, though a House bill reaches the Senate later -- and it set the document's own printed heading against the database's separate vocabulary, which spells the same thing differently. Compared on the text instead, all 24 publish the right words: 23 are word-identical to the newest printing once the document heading is discounted and one differs by 13 words. The two fiscal-note ones were real and are fixed -- the text was the introduced bill both times and only the label was wrong, which is the worse way round.
errors.guard: a bill's version is read from its own heading, not its fiscal note

errors.what: Interim study was described as returning a bill the following year, in two published places: The General Court on the Learn pages, and the tooltip on every bill card's 'carried over' chip. (A third copy, in build_pages.LEARN, is not published -- it is kept as the reference to diff civics.py against, and was corrected for that reason. How a bill becomes law names interim study only in a count of outcomes and was right.) It does not. Measured on all 16 dockets on disk: 1,429 'Retained in Committee' actions, 100.0% of them in the first year of a term; 4,465 interim-study actions, 95.9% in the second. Of 267 current-term bills sent to interim study, the only actions after the referral are the study's own work sessions that autumn -- none in a later year. A retained bill survives into the second year with its number; an interim-study bill dies with the term and must be refiled as a new bill.
errors.where: learn/general-court.html and the 'carried over' chip on every bill card; also the unpublished build_pages.LEARN reference copy

errors.guard: none -- it is a claim in prose and no check can read English. The docket measurement above is the thing to re-run if the rule is ever thought to have changed.

errors.what: Four statements on Testifying and attending were wrong or misleading. Filling in a card is how the HOUSE asks to speak -- the Senate has one sign-in sheet with a column to tick. 'There is no fixed time limit' is wrong: no rule sets one, but chairs may and commonly do, typically the sponsor as long as they need and three minutes for everyone else. Saying the sign-ins 'are published after the hearing' read as though the bill's docket carried them; it does not, and they are in the General Court's own sign-in lookup. And 'you do not need to live in the district' described a district that does not apply, since committees hear bills for the whole state.
errors.reported_by: an experienced state legislator, reviewing the Learn pages for the person

errors.what: Members' pay was given as '$100 a year', which is the arithmetic rather than the fact. It is $200 for the two-year term, paid once, in January of the first year, less withholding -- so a reader was left expecting an annual payment that does not exist.
errors.where: learn/general-court.html and the Learn index blurb
errors.reported_by: an experienced state legislator, reviewing the Learn pages for the person

errors.what: The testifying page's diagram still said a speaker "fills in a card" after 7da7c35 had corrected that same claim in the prose above it. Filling in a card is the House; the Senate has one sign-in sheet with a column to tick. So a commit that fixed a sentence left the picture beside it saying the old thing -- the class of miss worth recording, because a diagram is where a reader looks first and it was not searched when the prose was.
errors.reported_by: found while adding a diagram to another Learn page, by reading the existing ones for their format
errors.guard: none -- prose again. The lesson is procedural: when a fact is corrected on a Learn page, grep civics.py's FLOW_ tables for it too, because they state the same facts in a different shape.

errors.what: The SB 2 section of the town meeting page said the deliberative session is where articles are debated and amended "and nothing is decided". RSA 40:13, III gives the first session all business other than voting by official ballot, and IV has it vote on amendments -- including the only chance to change a sum of money before the ballot. What is true is narrower: no article is passed or defeated there. A reader told nothing is decided has been told they can skip the one session that shapes the ballot. The default budget was also half described: RSA 40:13, XI(b) lets the governing body adjust it until the ballots are printed, the definition omitted the reduction for eliminated positions, and the page implied the default is automatic when the governing body may instead call one special meeting.
errors.reported_by: found while building the town meeting and SB 2 diagram, by checking the page's existing claims against RSA 40:13 on disk
errors.guard: none -- prose. The claims now cite the paragraph they rest on, so the next reader can check each one in place.

errors.what: The finding-your-representatives page said most people have more than one representative "because a House district is built out of whole towns and wards rather than drawn to equal population". The constitution requires both: Part II, Article 9 forbids the legislature to divide a town, ward or place and says representation "shall be as equal as circumstances will admit". The same page described a floterial as laid over towns "that each already elect their own representative"; it is laid over whole districts, often several towns sharing one seat, so a town like Sanbornton elects no representative of its own. It also omitted the seven districts that join a city's wards to neighbouring towns.
errors.reported_by: found while building the representation diagram, by checking the page against RSA 662 and the constitutional text reproduced in the CACRs on disk
errors.guard: partly. The count of places with several representatives is now a figure computed each build rather than a typed sentence, and the worked example is drawn from the map with a build stop if it stops illustrating a floterial. The prose claims about the constitution are cited to the article, not checked.
